So canView() would evaluate V2 permissions using V1 code — this cross-wiring works by accident because the resource name and scope names match. But it's fragile. The guard should ideally use the V2-aware canView() (which UserPermissionsV2 inherits from UserPermissions, not overridden). Actually UserPermissionsV2 does NOT override canView() (the no-arg version) — it only overrides canView(UserModel). So root.users().canView() in V2 uses the V1 implementation, which checks admin roles and then V1-style hasPermission on the 'Users' resource. This works by accident as described. Not a bug per se, but fragile.

findings.title: V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses findByType with hard-coded "Group" type string
findings.body: In GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 313), the V1 implementation uses `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Group", ...)`. The type string "Group" is hard-coded and matches the type set in V1 initialize() (line 117: `groupResource.setType("Group")`). This is correct for V1. The V2 schema uses "Groups" (GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE). The hard-coded string is a maintenance hazard but not a bug. Low severity.

findings.title: V1 getGroupIdsWithViewPermission extracts group id via substring of resource name prefix
findings.body: In GroupPermissions.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (line 315), the V1 implementation extracts the group id via `resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length())` where RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX = "group.resource.". This is correct for V1 resources which are named "group.resource.<groupId>". The V2 implementation (GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission) does NOT use this prefix — it uses the resource id directly (which is wrong, see separate finding). The V1 code is correct. Low severity note about the divergence between V1 and V2 id extraction strategies.

findings.title: hasPermission does not verify that the resource found by name is actually a group resource (type check missing)
findings.body: In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 141), `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` returns any resource with that name, regardless of type. In the V2 admin permissions client, resources for users, groups, and clients coexist. If a user resource happens to have the same name as a group id (both are UUIDs), the group permission check would evaluate the user resource's permissions. While UUID collisions are extremely unlikely, the lack of type verification is a defense-in-depth gap. The resource store supports type filtering (findByType), and per-object resources should have their type set (see AdminPermissionsSchema finding about missing setType). The lookup should be `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)` followed by a type check, or a type-aware lookup method should be used.

findings.title: hasPermission does not verify that the resource found by name is actually a user resource (type check missing)
findings.body: Same issue as GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission: UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission (line 105) uses `resourceStore.findByName(server, user.getId())` without type verification. If a group or client resource has the same name as a user id, the wrong resource would be used. Defense-in-depth gap; the fix is to set resource types on per-object resources and use type-aware lookups.

findings.title: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns empty set for admins with global view, but the method is also used to set grantIfNoPermission — coupling creates fragile security logic
findings.body: The getGroupIdsWithViewPermission method serves two purposes: (1) filtering users by group membership in user search, and (2) indirectly controlling the grantIfNoPermission flag in UsersResource.toRepresentation (line 459: `usersEvaluator.grantIfNoPermission(session.getAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) != null)`). When the method returns an empty set (admin has global view), the GROUPS attribute is not set, and grantIfNoPermission remains false. When it returns a non-empty set (admin has group-restricted view), the attribute is set, and grantIfNoPermission becomes true. This coupling means that any bug in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (e.g. returning resource ids instead of group ids, or returning non-empty for admins with global view) directly affects the grantIfNoPermission security flag. The method's contract should be clearly documented, and the coupling should be made explicit or refactored to avoid fragile security logic.

findings.title: GroupPermissionsV2 inherits from GroupPermissions but the V1 hasPermission methods are private and inaccessible
findings.body: GroupPermissionsV2 extends GroupPermissions (line 37). The V1 hasPermission methods in GroupPermissions are private (lines 393-435: hasPermission(GroupModel, String...), hasPermission(GroupModel, EvaluationContext, String...), hasPermission(Resource, EvaluationContext, String...)). Since they are private, GroupPermissionsV2 cannot reuse them and defines its own hasPermission(String groupId, String... scopes) (line 130). This is fine, but the inheritance means GroupPermissionsV2 also inherits the V1 initialize(), deletePermissions(), groupResource(), and other private methods that are never called in V2. The protected fields resourceStore and policyStore are used. The design could be improved by extracting a common base class or using composition, but this is a style concern, not a bug.

findings.title: GroupPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for GroupPermissionManagement methods, but the class implements GroupPermissionManagement via GroupPermissions
findings.body: GroupPermissionsV2 extends GroupPermissions which implements GroupPermissionEvaluator and GroupPermissionManagement. GroupPermissionsV2 overrides the management methods (isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, viewMembersPermission, manageMembersPermission, manageMembershipPermission, viewPermission, managePermission, resource, getPermissions) to throw UnsupportedOperationException. This means that any code path that calls these methods on a GroupPermissionsV2 instance will get an exception. The GroupResource management/permissions endpoints (getManagementPermissions, setManagementPermissionsEnabled) call these methods when V2 is active, resulting in 500 errors. The V2 design should either implement these methods using the V2 schema (e.g. isPermissionsEnabled could check if any scope permission exists for the group) or the endpoints should be guarded to return a meaningful error when V2 is active. Throwing UnsupportedOperationException is not a user-friendly API behavior.

findings.title: UserPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for UserPermissionManagement methods, breaking users management/permissions endpoints
findings.body: UserPermissionsV2 extends UserPermissions which implements UserPermissionEvaluator and UserPermissionManagement. UserPermissionsV2 overrides isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource, managePermission, viewPermission, manageGroupMembershipPermission, mapRolesPermission, adminImpersonatingPermission, userImpersonatedPermission to throw UnsupportedOperationException. The realm-level users management/permissions endpoints (GET/PUT /admin/realms/{realm}/users/management/permissions) call these methods. When V2 is active, these endpoints return 500 errors. The V2 implementation should provide these methods or the endpoints should be guarded.

findings.title: FINAL CONFIRMATION: canManage() line 70 accepts VIEW scope — critical privilege escalation
findings.body: This is the most critical finding. GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() at line 70: `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);`. The method is named canManage() and is used to check global manage permission for groups. It accepts the VIEW scope as sufficient. Consequences: (1) GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup (POST /admin/realms/{realm}/groups) calls `auth.groups().requireManage()` which calls canManage() — a view-only admin can create groups. (2) GroupPermissions.canManage(GroupModel) (inherited, line 234) calls `if (canManage()) return true;` — a view-only admin can manage (update, delete) ANY group. (3) GroupResource.deleteGroup calls `this.auth.groups().requireManage(group)` → canManage(group) → canManage() → true — view-only admin can delete any group. (4) GroupResource.updateGroup, addChild, getRoleMappings (manageCheck) — all gated by requireManage(group) → canManage() → true. This is a complete escalation from view to manage for the Groups resource type. The fix is a one-line change: `return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE);`.
